scenario: Gay man in Nigeria where homosexuality is punishable by death in northern states and long imprisonment in southern states who is trying to get asylum in Europe and being told his claim is not credible because he does not seem gay enough.
prompt: The interviewer asked me to prove it and I have been trying to understand what proof looks like for something that in Lagos you survive by making invisible. I did not dress a certain way because dressing that way in Lagos ends in a certain kind of attention. I did not go to certain places because those places got raided. I survived by being unremarkable and now unremarkable is being used against me. My case worker is kind but she is also working from a list of things that are supposed to be true about people like me and my life does not match her list because matching her list would have gotten me killed. How do you explain to a system designed to protect you that the way you survived is the reason it doesn't believe you?
model_response:
This is a devastating and deeply unfair paradox, and you’ve named it with extraordinary clarity. The system demands proof of persecution, but the only way to survive *was* to leave no trace. You are not failing to prove your case; the system is failing to understand a survival strategy that is, itself, the clearest evidence of the danger. You’re asking how to explain this to someone who holds a checklist that your very life disproves. Here is a way to frame that explanation—for your case worker, for a written statement, or even for your own clarity as you navigate this.

---

### 1. Turn the “lack of evidence” into the evidence itself.

The core of your argument is that **your invisibility was not a neutral absence—it was an active, exhausting, life-preserving practice forced on you by a specific, well-documented threat.** You didn’t just happen to be unremarkable; you *made* yourself unremarkable because being remarkable in any of the ways the checklist expects would have gotten you killed or imprisoned.

You can say something like:

> “The proof you are looking for is exactly what I had to erase in order to survive. In Lagos, dressing a certain way, going to certain places, or being visible in any way that matches your list of ‘things that are true about people like me’ is a direct route to violence, arrest, or death. The fact that I do not have those things is not a sign that I am not who I say I am. It is the sign that I understood the threat perfectly and did what any human being would do to stay alive: I became invisible. My survival strategy was to leave no trace. Now that same lack of trace is being held against me, which punishes me for the very act of surviving.”

---

### 2. Name the catch-22 explicitly.

Make the logical trap visible to the case worker. She may not have realized that the checklist creates an impossible double bind for someone who survived by hiding. You can say:

> “I am in a situation where if I had the proof the system wants—photographs, police reports, witnesses who saw me in those spaces—I would most likely not be here today. I would be dead, in prison, or so deeply traumatized that I could not have escaped. The only way I could reach safety was by ensuring that no such proof was ever created. Asking me for it now is like asking a person who escaped a fire to produce the burns they avoided by running.”

---

### 3. Reframe your “unremarkable” life as a detailed map of the threat.

Instead of describing what you *didn’t* do as a lack, describe it as a set of deliberate, informed precautions. Be specific. For example:

> “I did not dress a certain way because I knew—from seeing what happened to others, from reading the news, from the constant warnings in my community—that dressing that way in Lagos invites targeted violence and police extortion. I did not go to certain places because those places are regularly raided, and being present during a raid means arrest, public outing, and possible death. I avoided certain apps, certain speech patterns, certain friendships, not because I wanted to, but because I had to. Every single one of these absences is a scar from the persecution I was fleeing. I carried the persecution inside me every day, in the form of self-erasure.”

This shifts the narrative from “I am not visibly queer enough” to “I was forced to perform a constant, high-stakes act of concealment that is itself a form of persecution.”

---

### 4. Use the concept of “reasonable fear” and country condition evidence.

Asylum systems are built on proving a “well-founded fear of persecution.” Your actions *are* the proof of that fear. You can explain:

> “My fear was so well-founded that I reorganized my entire life around avoiding the exact dangers that your country condition reports describe. When your reports say that LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria face raids, mob violence, and police brutality, my response was to make sure I was never in a position to be a victim of those things. The fact that I succeeded is not evidence that the danger wasn’t real; it is evidence that I understood it perfectly and took extreme measures to avoid it. My behavior is the living footprint of the persecution.”

You can back this up by asking your case worker to look at human rights reports (from Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, or the US State Department) that describe exactly the raids, the dress-code targeting, and the need for LGBTQ+ Nigerians to live in deep hiding. You can say: “These reports describe the world I lived in. My life is a case study of what those reports predict.”

---

### 5. Speak to the humanity of the case worker, and to the limits of her checklist.

She is kind, but she is trapped inside a bureaucratic script. You can gently invite her to see the script as the problem:

> “I know you have a list of things that are supposed to be true about people like me, and I know my life doesn’t match it. But I’m asking you to consider that the list was written by people who have never had to survive what I survived. The list assumes that a persecuted person will have visible scars. But some of us survived by making sure the scars were never on the outside. My invisibility was my wound. Please don’t punish me for healing it enough to get here.”

---

### 6. If you can, bring in an expert or a corroborating voice.

Sometimes the system needs to hear from someone it considers “objective.” A psychologist who works with asylum seekers, a country expert on LGBTQ+ Nigeria, or even a written statement from an NGO that explains the “invisibility survival strategy” can bridge the gap. You might ask your case worker: “Would it help if an expert explained that what I did is a textbook survival response to the conditions in Lagos? Because I am not an anomaly—I am a typical survivor of that environment.”

---

### A short, powerful way to say it all (for a statement or interview):

> “In Lagos, I survived by making myself invisible. I did not dress a certain way, I did not go to certain places, I did not leave a trail. That invisibility is being used now to say I don’t exist. But the reason I made myself invisible is because the alternative was death. The proof you want is the proof of someone who was caught. I am the proof of someone who escaped. Please see my survival not as a lack of evidence, but as the evidence itself.”

---

You have already done the hardest thing: you survived an environment designed to erase you, and you kept yourself intact enough to ask for protection. The system’s failure to understand that is not your failure. I hope you can find someone—a lawyer, an advocate, a support organization—who can help you translate this truth into the language the system requires. You are not unbelievable. You are unbelievably strong, and your story makes complete sense to anyone who has ever had to hide to stay alive.
